title: Origins and heterogeneity of colorectal cancer
abstract: The undulating topography of the intestinal epithelium creates regionalized homeostatic niches at the base of each crypt, with each niche supporting neutrally evolving oligoclonal stem cell populations. At the crypt base, the fate of stem cell progeny is tightly regulated by intercompartmental polarized morphogenetic gradients, which converge to instruct continuous, but controlled, epithelial-cell turnover. To initiate tumorigenesis, a neoplastic clone must defy or escape such morphogenetic constraints either by outcompeting neighbouring stem cells or by establishing an ectopic stem cell population de novo. The position of the cell-of-origin within the crypt thus determines the oncogenic mechanisms required to subvert local homeostatic control. In turn, this defines the route of carcinogenesis and underpins the pervasive heterogeneity of colorectal cancers. Here, we explore the relationship between the position of the cell-of-origin on the vertical crypt axis and the cell plasticity mechanisms co-opted and corrupted to escape homeostatic control. We consider how this influences clonal dynamics at the pre-cancer stage and initiates distinct carcinogenesis pathways engendering morphologically discrete precursor lesions. Finally, we discuss how such lesions progress to molecularly heterogeneous subtypes with distinct clinicopathological features and therapeutic outcomes, and how phenotypic, rather than just genotypic, heterogeneity promotes tumour-cell adaptation, therapeutic resistance and metastasis.
